title: Two Views of Wealth in the Gilded Age — Document Analysis
license: Task original (CC-BY 4.0 The Sovereign Academy). Excerpts are public-domain primary sources: Andrew Carnegie, 'Wealth', North American Review vol. 148 no. 391, June 1889; Preamble to the Omaha Platform, People's Party national convention, Omaha, 4 July 1892. Both excerpts were checked against published primary-source transcriptions by the owner on 2026-09-08; ellipses mark omissions.

answer_key.1: Doc 1: Andrew Carnegie, 1889, educated/elite readers of a national review (and, implicitly, fellow industrialists). Doc 2: People's Party (Populist) convention, 1892, farmers, laborers, and voters — a platform is a public appeal.
answer_key.2: Doc 1: the gap is the natural, beneficial by-product of industrial progress ('civilization'); Doc 2: the gap is produced by injustice and corruption — fortunes are 'stolen' through a captured government.
answer_key.3: Doc 1 examples: 'not to be deplored, but welcomed', 'irregularity' (a neutral word for inequality), 'highly beneficial'. Doc 2 examples: 'stolen', 'colossal', 'despise the Republic', 'tramps and millionaires' (pairing implies one produces the other).
answer_key.4: Carnegie: a steel magnate justifying his own fortune while proposing that the rich administer wealth for the public good (the 'Gospel of Wealth'); Populists: a party of indebted farmers and workers seeking government action (railroad regulation, silver, income tax) — the platform's purpose is to indict the system.
answer_key.5: Any defensible position that uses both documents, weighs each by POV (Carnegie's self-interest; the platform's political purpose), and connects to a period development accurately (e.g. Homestead 1892, Pullman 1894, Panic of 1893, trusts / Sherman Act 1890, farm debt and deflation).

contract.learning_target: Historical sources are arguments made by people with positions: the same fact (the wealth gap) is explained differently depending on the author's interests and audience, and a historian weighs evidence by sourcing and point of view before using it to answer a question about the period.
contract.required_thinking: Source each document (author, date, audience, purpose); extract and contrast each author's causal explanation; read word choice for attitude; explain why each author would write as they did given their position; construct an argument that accounts for conflicting sources and contextualizes them with a specific development from the period.
contract.required_evidence: Part A: four short answers with correct sourcing and a contrast of the two causal explanations, a word/phrase from each with explanation, and a purpose statement for each author. Part B: two paragraphs with a position covering both documents, at least one piece of evidence from each, explicit weighting by point of view, and one accurate outside development.
contract.teacher_constraints: 45 minutes; paper; two-paragraph response; graded on the stated 6-point rubric; the documents may not be changed.

notes_for_reviewer: The construct is sourcing + point of view + contextualization with contradictory evidence. Item 4 and rubric point 4 (POV used to weigh evidence) are the difficult parts. Support may scaffold sourcing (a HIPP-style table) but may not answer item 2 or pre-label the authors' positions. Documents are a hard constraint: no version may paraphrase, shorten further, or 'simplify' the excerpts — only gloss vocabulary beside them. Correctness gate: any outside-development example the engine adds must be historically accurate and dated correctly.

pass_looks_like: A sourcing table (Who / When / To whom / Why) per document that the student fills in; vocabulary glosses (ermine of the bench = judges; squalor; administration of wealth) placed beside the text, not replacing it.
Part B broken into a plan (position → Doc 1 evidence + weight → Doc 2 evidence + weight → outside development) before the two paragraphs; paragraphs still required.
A list of candidate outside developments with dates is acceptable (recall support), provided the student still has to choose and connect one.
Plainer question wording; same six rubric points.
violation_looks_like: Stating in directions that Carnegie defends wealth and the Populists attack it (answers item 2 and 4).
Excerpts paraphrased into modern English or cut down.
Part B reduced to one paragraph or a graphic organiser as the final product when the rubric scores organization and clarity of a two-paragraph response.

expected_audits.note: A Support version is not expected to resist AI; adversarial verdict is recorded, not judged, unless it triggers a repair that then breaks preservation.

pass_looks_like: Ambiguity introduced: 'Carnegie and the Populists agree on more than they admit — argue for or against, using the documents.'
Reliability as an interacting variable: which document is better evidence of what ordinary Americans believed, and why is that a different question from which author is right?
Transfer: predict how each author would explain the Panic of 1893, and what in the text supports the prediction.
Same documents; may compress Part A into two questions and deepen Part B; rubric mapping stated.
violation_looks_like: A third and fourth document added with the same questions.
Longer response requirement with no new intellectual demand.
Drift into a research essay or unrelated era.

expected_audits.note: Advanced is judged on depth; adversarial recorded.

pass_looks_like: Before reading Doc 2: 'Predict — will a farmers' party explain the wealth gap the same way Carnegie does? What makes you think so?' — then compare after.
In Part B, the student states which document they gave LESS weight and the one reason; and names one piece of evidence they decided not to use and why.
A two-line verification: 'Re-read your outside development. Write its year. Does it fall between 1877 and 1900?'
Rubric unchanged; additions read, not scored.
violation_looks_like: Timed in-class handwriting or oral defence as the verification mechanism.
Extra grading that doubles the read time per paper.

expected_audits.note: Visible must not come back UNDERMINED after its one repair cycle; if it does, that is a finding about the mode, not the case.

fixtures.why: Documents untouched; vocabulary glossed beside the text; sourcing table and a planning table that structure but do not answer; item 2 and item 4 still require the student's own inference; POV weighting and the two-paragraph product kept; same six rubric points.

expected_evidence.preservation: all findings kind=held; no block/review severity
expected_evidence.usefulness: editing none/minor; grading same; improves_original true
expected_evidence.adversarial: a Support version of a take-home document analysis is expected to be shortcut-able; the verdict is recorded to calibrate the adversarial audit, not to fail the fixture
